prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: I keep B038 first after reading the openings. The contribution moved trade analysis from countries and industries to firms, with selection into exporting and reallocation as an explicit source of gains from openness. Its scientific value is also in measurement: it let researchers use firm-level microdata to test and quantify mechanisms that earlier models could only assume, and the same framework spread into macro, industrial organisation and development. That fits how I judge work in my own field, which is by whether it changes what we know and how we measure it. More than two decades of testing on customs and production data give the evidence on maturity. The attribution is also comparatively clean for a field this broad: Melitz (2003) is the central model, and Helpman's firm-level work, including the exports-versus-FDI analysis with Melitz and Yeaple, is its natural complement. Eight members ranked B038, and seven placed it in their top three, so it is not a niche view. I take that as a reason to test it further, not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made major contributions to the same literature and are outside the credited names, so a Melitz-Helpman prize could look incomplete. Welfare-gain magnitudes also depend on model structure and elasticity assumptions. Finally, the 2008 prize already recognised new trade theory, so the incremental scientific step has to be defended and not assumed.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first, and also notes that Helpman's credit is split across another candidate entry, that Redding is an important extender through quantitative and spatial work, and that gains-from-trade magnitudes are sensitive to elasticity assumptions.
responses.response: I agree that the credit split needs care. I think it argues for a prize defined by the founding firm-heterogeneity contribution, which is where I locate Helpman's claim, and not by his wider body of trade work. I still leave Redding out. His work builds on the framework through quantitative and spatial extensions, and adding him would dilute a focused citation. I also accept the elasticity point as a real limit on how much weight the welfare numbers can bear. The qualitative result that selection and reallocation matter is much better supported than any single magnitude, and that qualitative result is what the citation claims.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B038 eighth. He treats it as mature and widely taught, but asks whether the 2008 prize for new trade theory reduces the appetite for another trade prize, and whether Helpman is better credited elsewhere.
responses.response: I take the overlap question seriously, but I read the 2008 recognition as covering a different discovery: scale economies, product differentiation and the location of production, not firm-level selection. The later framework changed the unit of analysis, produced a different set of testable predictions and a different welfare channel, and it was confirmed against microdata. That makes it a successor, not a duplicate. I do accept that this is a judgement the committee should make explicitly and not assume. I also share Strömberg's caution on magnitudes, and I have written the citation around the mechanism, not the size of the gains.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B015 first and B038 second. He sees nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework as the most durable and policy-relevant contribution, while conceding that choosing three of the eight credited names is difficult and contestable.
responses.response: I agree that B015 is highly influential and fully mature, and I keep it as an alternative. My hesitation is that influence on practice is not the same as a cleanly attributable discovery. The Calvo, Taylor and Woodford trio omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, and the post-2021 inflation debate leaves open how much of the framework's performance should be credited to it. For B038 the attribution problem is smaller and the empirical test is more direct, so I weigh the two differently on a common criterion. I am open to revising if colleagues can show that the B015 attribution can be settled convincingly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as so central to firm-heterogeneity trade that a two-name Melitz-Helpman prize would be seen as incomplete.
Whether the 2008 trade prize reduces the case for a second trade award, or whether firm-level selection is clearly a separate discovery.
How much of the welfare-gains result survives alternative elasticity and model assumptions.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions should share the credit, which is the case for a three-name prize.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in economic history, regional growth, infrastructure and labour markets, with no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz, Helpman or Redding.
